transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, thank you so much for seeing me. Yes, well, it's actually been a long time coming, I suppose. I'm a secondary school teacher—I teach history, mostly the older students, so I've been doing this a long time—and what really brought me in today is this... well, this habit I have where I just cannot seem to stay in my seat. 

It's getting a bit embarrassing, to be honest with you. We have these long faculty meetings, you know how administrative things go, the principal just goes on and on, and all the other teachers are just sitting there politely, taking notes or at least pretending to listen. But I keep getting up. I'll just suddenly feel this overwhelming urge to... I don't know, go refill my coffee, even if my mug is still perfectly warm and half full. Or I'll just stand up and walk all the way to the back of the room to check a stack of handouts on the back table that I already have a copy of right in front of me. 

And it's not just at school, either! It happens at dinner, too. When we have friends over or go out to a nice restaurant, everyone will be seated, having a lovely conversation, and I'll just pop up. I'll make up some excuse, like I need to go ask the hostess something or I need to check if the car is locked, even though absolutely nothing is actually urgent. I just... I get up. And then I look around and realize I'm the only person standing in the middle of a perfectly calm dinner, and I just don't understand why I can't just sit and be still like everyone else.
Can you recall whether this restlessness and difficulty staying seated has been present since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

Oh, goodness, no, it's definitely not a recent thing. Not at all. In fact, if you were to ask my mother—well, bless her heart, she passed a few years ago—but if she were here, she’d laugh right out loud at that question. She used to joke, and I mean she told this story at practically every family gathering, that I wore a permanent path in the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old. You know those old metal ones they used to screw into the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? The ones you really had to crank? I was always, always up sharpening my pencil. It didn't even need sharpening half the time, I just needed an excuse to be on my feet! 

And it wasn't just my mother noticing it, either. A few years back, I actually found a box of my old things when my husband and I were clearing out her attic, and my old primary school report cards were tucked away in this little pink folder. Every single one of them, year after year, the teachers would write these very polite notes saying I was a very bright girl, very capable, but—and there was always a 'but'—they said I simply could not stay in my seat. That, and I couldn't wait my turn. I was always popping up, blurting things out, just completely unable to stay anchored to my chair, exactly like I do now at those faculty meetings I was telling you about. 

So, yes, it has absolutely been there my whole life. I suppose when you're a child, people just write it off as you being a bit spirited or restless, and I really thought I would just naturally grow out of it as I matured and settled into my career. But here I am at sixty, still acting like that little girl who can't just sit quietly and listen to the lesson. It's just so frustrating to look back and realize it's been the exact same story for five decades.

latest_inference.note: Childhood onset with lifelong history of hyperactivity, impulsivity (blurting out, can't wait turn), and inability to stay seated documented across multiple settings (school reports, current work meetings, social settings) strongly supports ADHD, hyperactive-impulsive presentation. This lifelong, pervasive pattern since before age 12 rules out anxiety disorders (F41.1), medication-induced akathisia (G25.81), and specific phobia (F40.1), which would have later onset or situational triggers rather than a consistent developmental history.
